Sujit Telagamsetty on Instagram: "Sometimes, it’s not laziness.
It’s not lack of motivation.
And it’s not “just stress.”

It may be your thyroid.

You wake up tired,
even after sleeping.

Your body feels heavy.
Your mind feels slow.

You struggle to concentrate.
You forget simple things.

Your mood changes.
You feel irritated.
Then suddenly, you feel low.

And sometimes, you don’t even understand
why you feel this way.

Your weight may change.
Your sleep may change.
Your energy may disappear.

Even small daily tasks
can start feeling exhausting.

And the hardest part?

People around you may not understand.

They may say,
“Why are you so tired?”
“Why are you overthinking?”
“Just be positive.”

But you know something feels different.

Thyroid hormones affect many systems in the body, including energy, metabolism and mood. 
When thyroid function is too low or too high, it can affect how you feel and function every day.

So if your body feels different,
don’t blame yourself.

Listen to it.

Get the right evaluation.
Get your thyroid checked when appropriate.
And most importantly

stop calling yourself weak
for struggling with something
your body may be struggling to regulate.

Your symptoms are worth understanding.
You deserve answers, not judgment. ❤️

If symptoms persist, speak with a qualified healthcare professional rather than self-diagnosing.

Experiencing any of these symptoms?

I’ll personally reply and help you understand what your body might be telling you.

Dr. Rhonda Patrick on Instagram: "Some magnesium supplements make the dose look much larger than it really is.

This bottle advertises 400 milligrams per capsule. But look at the Supplement Facts panel: it says “magnesium citrate, 400 milligrams.” It never separately tells you how much elemental magnesium that it provides.

Magnesium citrate includes both magnesium and citrate. Four hundred milligrams of the entire compound is not 400 milligrams of magnesium. The Supplement Facts panel is supposed to disclose the magnesium amount, not substitute the weight of the entire compound.

It also says “Daily Value not established.” But magnesium absolutely has an established Daily Value. That is another warning sign that this panel is not clearly declaring the mineral dose.

Compare that with this other bottle: “Magnesium, as magnesium glycinate, 120 milligrams, 29% Daily Value.” That clearly identifies the amount of magnesium and the form supplying it.

This is an example of how magnesium labels can fool people. I don’t think it should be allowed. But now you are informed and can check your magnesium supplement as well as other mineral supplements you may have at home."

Idris | Online Fitness Coach on Instagram: "How to Smith Chest Press Correctly (Avoid These Chest Press Mistakes!!)
Smith Machine Bench Press

🎯 Target Muscles:
Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, Triceps Brachii

▶ STARTING POSITION | ATHLETE

1. Adjust the bench height so that when you lie down, the Smith machine bar is aligned with your nipple line. Make this adjustment before starting the exercise.
2. Lie on the bench and maintain 5 points of contact: both feet, glutes, upper back, and head.
3. Grip the bar with a pronated grip (palms facing forward). Position your hands slightly wider than shoulder width and wrap your thumbs around the bar.
4. Unhook the bar from the Smith machine and position it directly over your chest, aligned with your nipple line.

▼ ACTION

5. Maintaining the 5 points of contact, lower the bar under control toward your chest, keeping it aligned with the nipple line. Do not drop or bounce the bar off your chest.
6. As you lower the bar, keep your upper arms approximately 45° from your torso, with your forearms remaining roughly perpendicular to the floor.
7. Press the bar upward along the same path until you return to the starting position, with your elbows nearly or fully extended.
8. Control the bar throughout the entire movement and do not allow your shoulders to lose their stable position.

📚 Source: National Strength and Conditioning Association (NSCA)

Sujit Telagamsetty on Instagram: "We called it useless. But your appendix may be secretly protecting your gut

But science is telling us a more fascinating story. ❤️

Did you know your appendix contains beneficial gut bacteria?

This tiny organ may act as a safe house for your gut microbiome, protecting certain bacteria within structures called biofilms.

And here’s where it gets interesting.

When infections or severe diarrhea disturb your gut bacteria, your appendix might help restore the balance.

Emerging human research suggests this possibility, although scientists are still investigating how it works.

Your appendix might be more than just an organ we can live without.

Sometimes, the smallest parts of our body hold the most surprising secrets.

Retirement planning isn’t simply about assuming a fixed return and calculating how much money you need. 📊

Markets don’t always perform as expected. 📉📈 A well-structured retirement strategy should account for several moving parts:

🎯 Inflation-adjusted returns — Your future expenses may be significantly higher than today.

📊 Conservative return assumptions — Don’t build your entire retirement plan around assuming 12% returns every year.

🔄 Periodic review & rebalancing — Your portfolio and risk level may need to change over time.

💰 Tax-efficient investing — Taxes can significantly impact how much of your returns you actually keep.

🧾 Tax advantages — Make appropriate use of available tax-advantaged accounts and strategies.

💵 Withdrawal strategy — Plan which assets to withdraw first and how much to withdraw.

🪣 Bucket strategy — Separate your near-term, medium-term and long-term financial needs.

🏥 Changing expenses — Healthcare, housing, travel and lifestyle expenses can change significantly during retirement.

📉 Market volatility — Prepare for years when markets decline instead of assuming consistent growth.

🔍 Regular reviews — Your goals, income, risk tolerance and circumstances can change.

The goal isn’t to predict exactly what the future will look like. 🔮

The goal is to build a retirement plan that can adapt when reality doesn’t go according to plan. 🧭

⚠️ Important: These strategies are not suitable for everyone. Your retirement plan should consider your individual goals, time horizon, risk tolerance, financial situation and tax circumstances.

Ray Dalio on Instagram: "Productivity matters most in the long run, but credit matters most in the short run. This is because productivity growth doesn't fluctuate much, but debt does—allowing us to consume more than we produce when we acquire it, and forcing us to consume less when we have to pay it back.

Think of borrowing as simply a way of pulling spending forward. You are essentially borrowing from your future self, creating a time in the future where you must spend less than you make. Anytime you borrow, you create a mechanical, predictable cycle. This is as true for an individual as it is for the economy.

Credit isn't necessarily bad; it's bad when it finances overconsumption, but it's good when it efficiently allocates resources and produces income so you can pay back the debt. But remember, if the cycle goes up, it eventually needs to come down.

Dr. Rhonda Patrick on Instagram: "Could declining sex hormones help explain why we lose strength with age?

In a nationally representative study of 4,330 U.S. adults, grip strength peaked around age 35. After 70, the estimated age-related decline became steeper: approximately 1.1% per year in men and 1.5% in women.

Three findings stood out:

1. Hormone availability mattered. An estimate of testosterone available to tissues was more consistently associated with strength than total testosterone, in both men and women.

2. Estradiol was also linked to strength. Both total and estimated bioavailable estradiol were associated with grip strength in middle-aged and older women.

3. Older women who had used menopausal hormone therapy had stronger grips. Among women 65 and older, those with a history of hormone therapy had approximately 1.9 kilograms greater grip strength than never-users. Among women 80 and older, the difference was approximately 14%.

This was a cross-sectional study: researchers compared people of different ages rather than following the same individuals over time. It cannot establish that declining hormones caused strength loss or that hormone therapy prevented it. Other differences between hormone users and nonusers could help explain the findings.

Hormone therapy’s potential role deserves closer study. But we already have powerful tools for building muscle and strength including progressive resistance training and adequate protein intake. Those remain the foundation.

I covered this study, published in the Journal of Applied Physiology, in this week’s research newsletter. If you are not already signed up to my free weekly email newsletter you ate missing out. You can sign up at foundmyfitness.com/newsletter"
